titleEn: He heals the broken in heart
progression: | C G | Am F | C G | C C |
intro: One of the six psalms said every morning in the opening section of the service, where the last five of the book are recited in order. It is built as three stanzas, each opening with a fresh call to praise at verses 1, 7 and 12, and each running the same circuit: something enormous, then something small and particular. Stars get counted and broken hearts get bandaged in consecutive verses. For a learner the psalm is a gallery of participles, the form that names God by what He is doing rather than by what He did, and almost every line of the first stanza begins with one.

stichs.en: Praise the LORD.
For it is good to make music to our God;
for it is pleasant, and praise is fitting.

verses.summary: Three reasons to sing and none of them is that God needs it. Good, pleasant and fitting are claims about the act itself, which is an unusual way to open a hymn.

stichs.en: The LORD is the builder of Jerusalem;
He gathers in the outcasts of Israel.

verses.summary: The first thing said about God after the call to praise is construction work and repatriation. Both verbs describe repair of something already broken rather than creation from nothing.

stichs.en: The one who heals the broken in heart,
and binds up their wounds.

verses.summary: Bandaging is manual work with a physical object. Placed between rebuilding a city and naming the stars, it keeps the scale of the psalm from settling anywhere.

stichs.en: He counts the number of the stars;
to all of them He calls out names.

verses.summary: Counting is a bureaucratic act; naming is an intimate one. The verse does both to the same objects in the same breath, and the objects are the least personal things in the sky.

stichs.en: Great is our Lord and abundant in strength;
of His understanding there is no number.

verses.summary: The word for number appears here for the second time in two verses, and reverses. He assigns a number to the stars and there is none that fits Him.

stichs.en: The LORD sustains the lowly;
He brings the wicked down to the ground.

verses.summary: Two directions in one line, and the stanza closes on the moral order rather than the physical one. The lowly are raised without being said to deserve it.

stichs.en: Sing out to the LORD with thanks;
make music to our God on the lyre.

verses.summary: The second stanza opens the way the first did, with a plural imperative, but this time an instrument is named. The verb is the one used for singing back to someone who has sung first.

stichs.en: The one who covers the heavens with clouds,
who prepares rain for the earth,
who makes grass sprout on the mountains.

verses.summary: Three participles and one process traced from top to bottom: cloud, then rain, then what the rain produces. The mountains are the last place a farmer would irrigate and the first place this psalm looks.

stichs.en: He gives the animal its food,
to the young ravens that call.

verses.summary: The grass of the previous verse becomes food, and the chain ends with the least useful bird in the list of clean and unclean animals. Nothing here is fed because it is worth feeding.

stichs.en: He does not delight in the strength of the horse,
He takes no pleasure in the thighs of a man.

verses.summary: Cavalry and infantry, named by the body parts that do the work. After feeding ravens, the psalm says what God is not impressed by, and it is the entire military budget of an iron age state.

stichs.en: The LORD takes pleasure in those who fear Him,
in those who wait for His kindness.

verses.summary: The same verb from the previous verse, now positive. What replaces strength is not a different kind of strength but waiting, which is the absence of action.

stichs.en: Praise the LORD, Jerusalem;
praise your God, Zion.

verses.summary: The third stanza opens and the imperatives are feminine singular, addressed to a city. From here to the end the psalm speaks to Jerusalem rather than about her.

stichs.en: For He has strengthened the bars of your gates;
He has blessed your children within you.

verses.summary: Security described from the inside of a walled town: the bar across the gate, then the children who are safe because of it. Both verbs are completed action, unlike the participles of the first two stanzas.

stichs.en: The one who sets your border as peace,
He satisfies you with the finest wheat.

verses.summary: The border is not defended, it is made of peace. Then food, because a besieged city and a hungry city are the same problem stated twice.

stichs.en: The one who sends His utterance to the earth;
very swiftly His word runs.

verses.summary: The word is given legs. What follows in the next three verses is the errand it was sent on, and it turns out to be the weather.

stichs.en: The one who gives snow like wool,
He scatters frost like ashes.

verses.summary: Two comparisons taken from a house rather than from nature. Snow in Jerusalem is rare enough to need explaining, and it gets explained by things on the floor of a kitchen.

stichs.en: He throws down His ice like crumbs;
before His cold, who can stand?

verses.summary: The domestic images go one step further and then break into a question. Cold is the only force in the psalm that nobody is said to survive.

stichs.en: He sends His word and melts them;
He makes His wind blow, and waters flow.

verses.summary: The thaw, done by the same word that ran to the earth in verse 15. Winter is not defeated by heat here but by speech, and the whole cycle takes four verses.

stichs.en: He tells His words to Jacob,
His statutes and His judgments to Israel.

verses.summary: The word that melted the ice is now the word given at Sinai, and the psalm makes the transition without a seam. One vocabulary covers physics and law.

stichs.en: He has not done so for any nation,
and as for judgments, they have not known them.
Praise the LORD.

verses.summary: The last claim is exclusive and it is about law, not about weather or bread, which were given to everyone. Then the psalm closes with the same two words it opened with.

pardes.body: Three stanzas, each starting with an imperative to praise: {{1.0}} at the head, {{7.0}} at verse 7, {{12.0}} at verse 12. Each stanza then alternates scales without warning. Stanza one puts rebuilding a city, bandaging wounds and naming stars in three consecutive verses. Stanza two goes from cloud formation to ravens to the uselessness of cavalry. Stanza three narrows to one city and ends by saying that what she has been given was given to nobody else. Read straight through, the psalm never argues that the large and the small are connected. It simply refuses to separate them, line after line, until the refusal is the point.

The word for number in {{4.1}} comes back in {{5.6}} and turns over: the stars have one, God's understanding does not. That pair is the tightest piece of wordplay in the psalm and it survives translation badly. The verb in {{7.0}} is the ordinary root for answering, used here for song, which is why some renderings give sing responsively rather than simply sing. There is also a division worth knowing: in the Greek and Latin traditions this is two psalms, the break falling exactly at {{12.0}}, where the change to feminine singular imperatives and the shift from participles to completed verbs both happen. The Hebrew tradition keeps it as one, and the two numbering systems part company here.

The classic reading of this psalm hangs on the seam between verses 3 and 4. The one who counts the stars and gives each a name is the one who bandages the broken hearted, and the order matters: the wounds come first. Read that way, the astronomy is not there to impress but to establish that attention at that scale is possible, so that attention to one person is not a smaller claim. The end of the psalm has been read as a matching pair. Rain and bread in verse 8 and verse 9 go to everyone, animals included; the statutes of verse 19 go to one people. What is universal is subsistence, what is particular is instruction, and the psalm is careful not to confuse which is which.

In the kabbalistic vocabulary cold and contraction belong to the side of judgment and warmth and flow to the side of kindness, which makes verses 16 to 18 a compressed account of how a severe state resolves. The frost of {{16.2}} is scattered, the cold is unanswerable, and then a word is sent and everything melts and moves in {{18.2}}. Nothing is removed by force. A word arrives and the same substance that was locked becomes water. The last verse then reads as a statement about the vessel rather than the gift: {{20.4}} says the nations were not given this, and the reading takes that to mean not that they were denied something but that the instruction requires a form prepared to receive it.
